rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

All pairs have excess resolution, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed reveals how the critical pairs respond to gradient steepness.
The critical cluster responds strongly to gradient duration. An intermediate duration should recover much of its resolution while keeping the last peak substantially earlier than in injection 1.

Keep the near-optimal gradient and test temperature-dependent selectivity of the sole unresolved pair. Higher temperature should shorten retention and may raise that pair above R = 1.5 without introducing a time penalty.

The central peak pattern suggests the critical pair crossed between 40 and 50 C; moving to 55 C may separate it on the other side of that crossing. The neighboring gaps appear large enough to justify this test while retaining a short run.

Increase gradient steepness by about 4% to try to lift the nearly resolved, reordered central pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the neighboring separation. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window, and the run should stay below the time-penalty threshold.

A further modest increase in steepness should push the critical pair above R = 1.5, based on injections 5 and 6. The neighboring pair still has some resolution margin, and the shorter retention should preserve the zero time penalty.

Injection 7 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the best method. Test a slightly shallower gradient to improve the neighboring pair’s resolution while checking whether the critical pair stays at or above R = 1.5.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test whether a slightly higher starting organic fraction offers another fully resolved, shorter method. Comparing with injection 8 keeps gradient slope constant and probes the starting composition’s effect on the two closest pairs.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 9 to recover resolution of the new critical pair while retaining the improved separation of the other close pair. This may provide a maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins and no time penalty.

The maximum score is already achieved; explore a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to seek larger resolution margins. The shallower slope should offset compression of the earlier critical pair, while the last peak is expected to remain below the time-penalty threshold.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 11 to recover the earlier critical pair’s resolution while preserving the other pair’s margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially restoring CRF 1.000 with improved minimum resolution.

One more small slope reduction should balance the two closest pairs near R = 1.7 while keeping the last peak just below 10 minutes. This tests for stronger resolution margins at the already-achieved maximum CRF.

This grid combination gives a slope between injections 12 and 13, aiming to balance the two critical pairs with minimum resolution near 1.7. It should retain the maximum CRF while modestly shortening retention relative to injection 13.

With the maximum CRF secured, test the unexplored lower-temperature selectivity region against injection 3. Cooling may separate its critical pair, although the adjacent pair could become limiting; the last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient at 40 C to improve the slope-sensitive central pair, using a higher starting fraction to offset the added retention time. This explores an alternative maximum-score region while retaining the proven 55 C methods.

Raise the starting organic fraction one grid step from injection 16 to bring the last peak below 10 minutes and remove its small time penalty. The accompanying shallower slope may help preserve the critical pair’s resolution above 1.5.

Test whether a longer, shallower gradient improves the central pair’s resolution, with a higher starting fraction offsetting the added retention time. This may yield another maximum-score method with greater resolution margin, though the early pair and 10-minute time threshold need checking.

Return to the successful 55 C region and test a slightly shallower slope than injection 10. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty while checking a nearby alternative to the maximum-score methods.

Test a slope between injections 9 and 10 to shorten retention while aiming to keep both critical pairs above R = 1.5. The endpoint remains above the observed last-peak elution fraction, so all compounds should elute during the gradient.

Refine around injection 14 with a slightly steeper slope, aiming to balance both critical resolutions near 1.7 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests for a larger minimum-resolution margin.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 10 to increase the earlier critical pair’s separation while checking that the other remains fully resolved. This should provide another maximum-score option with more time margin than injection 21.

Test a slope between injections 12 and 21 to retain comfortable resolution margins while shortening retention relative to injection 21. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so this should preserve complete elution and the maximum CRF.

Use a slope between injections 21 and 23 with a tighter solvent window, targeting balanced critical-pair resolutions around 1.7. The last peak should still elute during the gradient near 9.3 minutes, preserving the maximum CRF.
